summary:
Terra Twin is a planetary terrain research platform designed to investigate morphological similarities and differences between the surfaces of the Moon and Mars using real NASA elevation datasets.

The platform integrates planetary terrain visualization, geospatial exploration, quantitative comparison, and statistical reliability analysis into one research environment. Using elevation data from NASA's Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) and Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA), Terra Twin extracts and compares terrain characteristics through statistical measurements, including the Terra Morphological Similarity Index (TMSI), Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistics, and Wasserstein distance.

The platform also evaluates result robustness through bootstrap confidence intervals, spatial autocorrelation, and sensitivity analysis.

Terra Twin aims to make planetary terrain research more accessible, transparent, and reproducible, supporting planetary science education and comparative geomorphology while helping users explore how different planetary landscapes can be quantitatively studied.
details:
Project Overview

Terra Twin is an interactive planetary terrain research platform that investigates morphological similarities and differences between planetary surfaces. It combines scientific data processing, geospatial visualization, quantitative comparison, and statistical validation.

How It Works

Terra Twin processes planetary elevation datasets from NASA missions to extract terrain characteristics and compare selected regions across planetary bodies.

The application contains five main sections:

1. EXPLORE

A terrain exploration workspace for examining lunar and Martian elevation data through terrain layers, elevation visualization, color ramps, and geographic controls.

2. COMPARE

A quantitative research workspace presenting the Terra Morphological Similarity Index (TMSI), confidence intervals, Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistics, Wasserstein distance, and feature distributions.

3. RELIABILITY

A statistical validation environment incorporating bootstrap confidence intervals, seed sensitivity, Moran's I spatial autocorrelation, and geographic extent sensitivity analysis to investigate the robustness of results.

4. DATA & METHODS

A scientific documentation section containing dataset inventories, data provenance, processing methodology, research findings, limitations, and data export capabilities.

5. MAP

A geographic research explorer presenting planetary candidate locations, coordinates, filtering capabilities, and location information.

Scientific Results

The current Moon–Mars comparison reports a Terra Morphological Similarity Index of 49.92, with a 95% confidence interval of 42.59–57.15. Additional reported measurements include a Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic of 0.492 and a Wasserstein distance of 8.539.

These measurements represent outputs of the project's analytical framework and should not be interpreted as proof of geological equivalence between planetary surfaces.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Terra Twin aims to make comparative planetary terrain investigation more accessible by bringing visualization, quantitative analysis, geographic exploration, and statistical reliability assessment into one platform.

Its potential applications include planetary science education, comparative geomorphology, research exploration, and investigating terrain characteristics relevant to future planetary exploration.

Technology and Tools

The project uses:

  • Python for scientific computation and data processing.
  • TypeScript for application development.
  • React and Next.js for the application interface and architecture.
  • Three.js for 3D terrain visualization.
  • Leaflet for interactive geographic mapping.
  • OpenStreetMap for geographic basemap tiles.
  • NASA Planetary Data System datasets, including LOLA and MOLA.

Creativity and Scientific Responsibility

Terra Twin goes beyond displaying planetary imagery by combining terrain visualization with quantitative morphological comparison and statistical reliability testing.

The project documents dataset provenance, methodological limitations, uncertainty, and the distinction between morphological similarity and geological equivalence.

AI-assisted development tools were used during implementation, debugging, and troubleshooting. NASA datasets and external software resources are attributed to their respective sources.
